hints: Remember what Fehling's solution is really testing for, aldehydes or ketones?
Look carefully at the end of each carbonyl group in P, Q and R to spot whether it is -CHO or -COCH3.
Any molecule containing at least one aldehyde group will give the red-brown precipitate, so check which structures qualify.
walkthrough:
**Recall what Fehling's does**

Fehling's solution is a mild oxidising agent. It oxidises aldehydes on gentle warming to give a red-brown precipitate of copper(I) oxide, $\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$. Ketones are not oxidised, so they give no precipitate and stay blue.

**Classify P, Q and R**

Look at what is attached to each $\text{C=O}$ carbon. If it has H attached, it is an aldehyde ($-\text{CHO}$). If it has two carbons attached, it is a ketone.

$$\text{P: CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CHO, Q: HOCCH}_2\text{CHO, R: CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{COCH}_3$$

**Decide who gives a positive test**

P has one ketone and one aldehyde group, so it is positive. Q has two aldehyde groups, so it is positive. R has two ketone groups only, so it is negative. Therefore P and Q only form the red-brown precipitate.

options.A: Incorrect. P and Q do react because they contain aldehyde groups, but R is a diketone with no -CHO group. Ketones resist oxidation by Fehling's, so R stays blue.
options.B: Correct. P is a keto-aldehyde and Q is a dialdehyde. Both contain at least one aldehyde group that is oxidised by Fehling's to give red-brown Cu2O. R is pentane-2,4-dione, a diketone only, so it gives no reaction.
options.C: Incorrect. P alone is incomplete. P is positive, but Q is also positive because it has two aldehyde groups. Students sometimes miss Q by misreading the structure.
options.D: Incorrect. Q alone is incomplete. Q is positive, but P is also positive because one end is -CHO even though the other end is a ketone. One aldehyde group is enough for a positive test.
